frameworks.name: Collective Bonus Pool Model
frameworks.definition: A team compensation structure where bonus payouts are tied to collective threshold achievement, aligning individual incentives with group performance.

claims.text: A bonus pool where all team members benefit only if collective revenue exceeds a threshold creates peer reinforcement: when one team member underperforms, others actively support them rather than compete, because the group succeeds or fails together. This reframes internal dynamics from individual ranking to collective achievement.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Bonus payout contingent on collective threshold
claims.mechanism: When bonus is collective, peer pressure shifts from competition to collaboration; underperformers become the team's shared problem to solve, not internal rivals to defeat.
bounded_by: Does not apply to roles where differentiation and individual commission are required

claims.text: Team unity and external enemy framing (competing against rival businesses rather than each other) produces better culture outcomes and faster collective scaling than internal competition-based bonus structures. The shift from cutthroat internal ranking to collective-enemy positioning is learned through iterations with larger teams.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Sales team at scale (multiple team members)
claims.mechanism: When the enemy is external (other businesses), team members stand side-by-side in trenches rather than competing for position; this configuration enables larger teams and higher team profits.
bounded_by: Hormozi's earlier approach was cutthroat internal competition; this evolved over time as team size and profitability increased

claims.text: Individual competitive drive (desire to win, not monetary incentive) is the psychological anchor that makes collective bonus pools effective. Alex Hormozi positions competitive spirit—the intrinsic motivation to beat external rivals—as independent of and deeper than monetary reward structures.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Collective bonus pool structure in place
bounded_by: Requires team members who are intrinsically competitive; does not assume money is the primary driver

examples.text: When one sales team member (Johnny) underperforms, the rest of the team proactively drills and coaches him to bring performance up, because all team members share in the bonus pool tied to collective revenue. This transforms underperformance from a ranking issue into a collaborative problem-solving moment; the team wants the entire group to succeed because their bonus depends on it.

Hormozi's evolution from early-stage cutthroat internal competition (where team members competed against each other directly) to a unified team-vs-external-rivals frame happened as the business scaled and profitability increased. The shift was not strategic decree, but discovery: larger teams and higher profits resulted from aligning incentives toward collective enemies rather than internal rank.

practices.text: Structure bonus payouts around a collective threshold that all team members must exceed together, not individual rankings or tiered commissions.
Position competitor businesses as the team's external enemy ('those guys are ripping off customers, let's put them out of business') rather than framing internal team members as rivals.
Ensure leadership personally models the cultural norm of process authority over individual discretion; Hormozi's example is his shift in philosophy from cutthroat to collective.
